$comment: Denied because each of these silently discards uncommitted work, and one of
them already did. A mutation sweep reverted each patch with
`git checkout -- <file>` from a tree whose implementation was not yet
committed; the first revert restored HEAD and destroyed it, and the twelve
mutations after it reported a missing anchor against a file that no longer
held the code. AGENTS.md already named the sibling hazard for `commit`; this
is the same class, and a deny rule fires at the moment of the mistake rather
than in a document read once at the start of a session.
`git switch` is deliberately NOT denied: branch work is legitimate and has a
non-destructive verb. To undo a change on purpose, commit first and revert,
or hold the original bytes and restore them -- which is what
a mutation harness must do instead of shelling out to git.
NOT VERIFIED, and the previous version of this comment claimed otherwise.
It said the refusal `was verified by attempting one denied form and
observing Claude Code refuse it`, and that the file is covered by
`tools/test_documentation.py`. Both were false when written.
What actually happened: the acceptance test ran `git checkout -- canary.txt`
against a canary file, and the command EXECUTED and destroyed it. Almost
certainly because permission settings bind at session start and the session
doing the testing predated this file -- but the rule under test was not
observed to fire, which is the only thing that would settle it. And no test
in this repository references this file at all: `test_documentation.py`
covers docs, ADR and changelog claims, and says nothing about settings.
So `AGENTS.md`'s rule is the load-bearing half today, and this list is a
belt whose buckle has never been pulled. Closing it needs a session that
starts after this file exists -- which now, on main, any fresh one does --
to attempt one denied form and observe the refusal. Until somebody has,
this comment says so, because a safety control that is only believed in is
the failure this repository keeps paying for.
